title: Should There be a Teacher In-the-Loop? A Study of Generative AI Personalized Tasks Middle School
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether teacher-in-the-loop use of generative AI can support personalized mathematics task design in middle school, and how that process affects both teacher workflow and student perceptions. The central question is whether teachers should remain involved when using large language models to adapt tasks to students’ interests, and whether such involvement leads to useful personalization or simply adds time and complexity.

Seven 7th-grade mathematics teachers used ChatGPT (with GPT-4o) to modify existing Illustrative Mathematics problems so they were more aligned with their students’ interests, especially popular culture references. The teachers participated in training on personalization, bias, readability, and cultural relevance, then worked through two curriculum units while prompting ChatGPT in Zoom sessions that were recorded and logged. Their 521 students completed the personalized assignments in ASSISTments and provided closed-ended ratings and open-ended feedback.

The study found that teachers used a wide range of prompts to adjust grain size, realism, age appropriateness, location, names, readability, and mathematical clarity. Students generally preferred finer-grained, specific references, while teachers often worked at broader interest categories and spent substantial effort correcting realism issues. Personalization took about 4 minutes per problem on average, and it did not become clearly faster over time; in fact, teachers used more prompts and more time in the second unit, although student ratings improved. The authors conclude that teacher-in-the-loop personalization can support professional learning and oversight, but it is time-intensive and may not achieve the small-grain personalization many students prefer.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory qualitative/mixed-methods study with descriptive and correlational analyses, not a randomized controlled trial. It provides useful evidence about teacher prompting and student reactions, but credibility is limited by the absence of a control group and reliance on observational data.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows modest positive effects on student interest ratings under certain prompting conditions, but the primary efficiency finding is negative and direct learning outcomes were not measured. Overall impact is unclear-to-modest for K-12 practice, especially beyond the specific middle school math context.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-in-the-loop use of ChatGPT/GPT-4o to personalize middle school mathematics word problems to students’ interests, including prompting, revising, and checking realism, readability, and mathematical clarity.

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily evaluates personalized middle school math problem creation, not direct achievement. Students’ ratings of the personalized problems’ interestingness and closeness to their interests were significantly higher when teachers used 3-5 prompts, by about 0.24 points on a 5-point scale (B=0.240, SE=0.085, t=2.84, p=0.0073). However, the study did not measure standardized math performance or learning gains, so evidence on numerical achievement remains indirect.
finding.measure: Student ratings of problem interestingness and closeness to interests on 1-5 scales
finding.std_deviation: SD=1.24 interestingness; SD=1.28 closeness for rating items; problem creation SD=2.6 prompts

finding.finding_summary: Students generally responded favorably to personalized math tasks when the popular-culture reference matched their interests, but disliked tasks when the reference did not match. Across 454 responses to the interestingness question, 163 implied the problem was interesting versus 243 implying it was not, and the paper reports slightly higher average ratings in Unit 6 than Unit 4 for interestingness (2.56 vs 2.27) and closeness (2.66 vs 2.28), with the increase statistically significant (B=0.33, SE=0.095, t=3.49, p=0.0012).
finding.measure: Student survey ratings of interestingness and closeness to interests; open-ended feedback on interest
finding.study_size: n=521 students; 454 open-ended responses for interest question
finding.std_deviation: Unit 4 interestingness SD=1.17; Unit 6 interestingness SD=1.26; Unit 4 closeness SD=1.20; Unit 6 closeness SD=1.29

finding.finding_summary: Teacher-facing personalization with ChatGPT was time-intensive rather than time-saving. Teachers used an average of 3.2 prompts per problem and spent about 246 seconds (roughly 4 minutes) per problem overall; in the second unit, time increased to 286 seconds per problem and prompts increased to 4.6 per problem, indicating no efficiency gains with iteration and a statistically significant increase in time (B=70.4 seconds, SE=29.6, t=2.38, p=0.0189).
finding.measure: Teacher time to create each personalized problem and number of prompts used
finding.std_deviation: SD=165.7 seconds per problem; SD=2.6 prompts per problem
